newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine grains futures seen growing, but slowly.
newsitem.headline: Argentine grains futures seen growing, but slowly.

text.p: Argentina's main grains futures exchange is slowly progressing with studies of how to boost its relatively puny trading volume but change is still a while off, a top National Securities Commission official said.

While Argentina's farms are fast modernizing and taking on an importance in world markets that had dwindled during decades of economic chaos, the Buenos Aires Futures Exchange, or Mercado a Termino de Buenos Aires, has lagged behind.

Agriculture Secretary Felipe Sola in June accused the exchange of dragging its feet on changes to boost its trading volume. The Agriculture Secretariat and the National Securities Commission began prodding the exchange to modernize at the end of 1994.
"We would like to see a market that trades four times our grain output," Commissioner Andres Hall told Reuters in a telephone interview.

This was a modest enough target, Hall said, pointing out that the Chicago Board of Trade, which is swollen by investors from around the globe hedging in the one market, trades up to 60 times the volume of U.S. soybean output.
He said that the Buenos Aires exchange only traded about a third of Argentina's 50-million tonne grain output in 1996. This was low but up from seven million tonnes the year before.
The exchange has made some reforms to increase liquidity, but much more remains to be done, Hall said.

"We would like to see the number of delivery locations reduced and perhaps the number of months as well," he said, "We would also like to see the Mercado a Termino change its trading hours to more closely match trading hours in Chicago."

Another major reform being pushed by the National Securities Commission and the government is for all four main products to be traded at the same time. The exchange currently trades maize, wheat, soybeans and sunflower seed one after the other in separate mini-sessions.
Prices are quoted for delivery to four grain ports.
"I don't know what the timetable will be (for changes to be made)," said Hall, "there are certain logistical problems."
One problem was that smaller brokers fear they would not have enough manpower to compete if all grains traded simultaneously.

Most of Argentina's grain output is traded off-floor, either in cash market trades or in an idiosyncratic contract known as "a fijar", or "price to be fixed", where grain to be delivered at a future date is priced according to an estimate of cash market values.

The government believes that the opaque nature of the cash market has allowed some prices, particularly of sunflower seed in Buenos Aires, to be manipulated. It hopes that more futures trading on a properly regulated exchange will remove irregularities and grant more financial security for farmers.

Argentina has a second, smaller futures exchange in Rosario. Many in the industry believe Rosario's easy access to the grainbelt makes it a more logical place than Buenos Aires for the country's main grains market, but the capital's financial and social weight have given it an advantage.
